newsitem.title: ESTONIA: SOCCER-WORLD CUP QUALIFIER ABANDONED AFTER THREE SECONDS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-WORLD CUP QUALIFIER ABANDONED AFTER THREE SECONDS.

text.p: A World Cup qualifying match between Estonia and Scotland was abandoned after three seconds on Wednesday when the hosts failed to turn up for the rescheduled start time.
Confusion surrounded who would be awarded the European group four match after 18 hours of protests and counter-protests over the kick-off time.
Initially Estonian officials said Scotland would be awarded a 3-0 victory, but the ultimate decision on who would be credited with a win rested with FIFA.
FIFA spokesman Keith Cooper said a decision probably would not be made until later this week at the earliest.

On Tuesday night, FIFA match delegate Jean-Marie Gantenbein ignored pleas from Scotland coach Craig Brown and Scottish Football Association officials that the temporary floodlights at the Kadriorg stadium were inadequate and that the game should be brought forward.
However, following further protests on Wednesday morning, FIFA ordered the start of the game to be rescheduled to 3 p.m. (1300 GMT) instead of the previous 6.45 p.m. (1545 GMT).
Brown said the lighting was the worst he had seen at an international fixture and gave the pitch a "gloomy and eerie atmosphere".
FIFA backed the Scots but the Estonian team did not turn out on the pitch at the appointed time.
The referee blew the whistle to start the match and after three seconds halted it.
Estonian Football Federation secretary-general Ainar Lettonon told Estonian radio the game was awarded to the Scots.

He later told Reuters that it had been impossible to get the Estonian team to the stadium on time from their training camp and arrange security as the Estonians only knew of the decision in the morning.
"I am not angry but I am very unhappy," he said.
He added that he had even talked to FIFA's secretary general Sepp Blatter, who had however backed the FIFA delegation decision's to start the game earlier.

"Of course we will acccept any decision made by FIFA but we have to make sure that the rights of every football association are respected," Lettonen added, saying he was "not sure" whether his association's rights had been respected.
Brown wanted the game to start earlier after he found that two temporary floodlight stanchions were at a different height from two permanent stanchions.
The Estonians said it was impossible to rearrange the match as all the tickets had been sold and live television coverage had been arranged.
Lettonen said his association could face a stiff fine or be excluded from FIFA although he doubted this would happen.
Though FIFA have yet to rule on the abandoned match, Lettonen said his association had sent a protest to the sport's world governing body on the basis that the Scots had been awarded a victory.
"We have sent the protest so we have done all that we can do," he said.
